Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 30
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Carpenter
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Tactile (Touch): Physical touch, Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event, Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overeat: eat excessively to manage distress, Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Vignette:
Michael is a 30-year-old North American male who has been experiencing significant psychological distress since he witnessed his friend's horrific accident at a construction site over three months ago. Michael had just joined his friend Jake on the job when they heard the loud screech of metal and saw Jake falling from an upper level, landing with a sickening thud below. The sight of Jake bleeding profusely and crying out in pain was seared into Michael’s memory. Since that fateful day, Michael has found himself struggling to cope with vivid flashbacks that are triggered by various stimuli. The most potent triggers include physical touch from his wife, the taste of a specific brand of coffee he had been drinking at the time of the accident, and the sight of injuries or wounds on others. These triggers often bring back the full memory of the traumatic event without warning, causing him to relive the horror as if it were happening all over again. Michael’s struggle is compounded by his inability to verbalize the experience. He can feel every aspect of the trauma—smelling the metal and concrete dust, hearing Jake's screams—but he cannot articulate these sensations in words. This nonverbal memory adds a layer of confusion and frustration as he tries to make sense of what happened. To manage his distress, Michael has turned to overeating and deliberate dissociation. He finds comfort in food, often eating large quantities even when not hungry, and will sometimes deliberately blank out or leave his body to escape the overwhelming memories. However, these maladaptive strategies only provide temporary relief and have led him to feel increasingly isolated from his wife and colleagues. Michael’s avoidance behaviors have become more pronounced over time. He tries to avoid thinking about the event altogether, which has resulted in a significant decrease in his work performance. The construction site where he witnessed Jake’s accident is now filled with triggers that make it nearly impossible for Michael to focus on his job. Consequently, he has missed several deadlines and received multiple warnings from his boss. The impact of these symptoms extends into his personal life as well. He avoids physical contact with his wife, which has strained their relationship. His wife feels frustrated by the distance and lack of intimacy, leading to frequent arguments that leave Michael feeling guilty but also further entrenched in his avoidance behaviors. Michael’s negative appraisals have taken a significant toll on his sense of self and outlook on life. He is certain that his life has been irrevocably altered by this trauma and finds it difficult to envision a future beyond the pain he experiences daily. The belief that he cannot rely on himself anymore exacerbates his anxiety, making him feel helpless in the face of everyday challenges. What frightened Michael most was the fear of never recovering from this event and losing all sense of who he once was. He had come to believe that he was permanently damaged and would never return to being the person he was before witnessing Jake’s accident. This belief has made it increasingly difficult for him to engage in activities he once enjoyed, further isolating him from his friends and family. Michael finally decided to seek help after a particularly distressing incident at work where he dissociated during an important meeting, leading to significant embarrassment and concern from his colleagues. He is most hoping that therapy can provide him with tools to manage his symptoms and find some semblance of normalcy in his life again. Michael’s fear now lies not just in reliving the trauma but also in losing touch with who he was before it happened and finding a way to reclaim his life despite the overwhelming memories and triggers.
